title: From waste collection to value recovery: why each photograph was chosen
overview: Each slide uses a realistic photograph as its base layer, in the way Recykal's EPR posts do, but keeps the DRS system: DRS green, uppercase headings, green call-outs and the standard footer. The four photographs follow the material through its journey: leaking out of the system, being returned, being handled, and being processed.
rules: Photographic base, DRS brand system: the photography treatment follows the EPR posts; colours, type and footer stay DRS.
All copy sits on a white fade over the photograph, on the left. The logo, headline and body never sit on the image itself.
Each photograph was generated with its subject on the right and a bright, quiet area on the left, so the fade is soft and the subject is never washed out. Fade width and text width are set per slide.

Four different settings (street, supermarket entrance, collection centre, and a recycling-plant bench) so no two slides repeat a scene. A light, shared colour grade ties them together; slide 4 is the darkest because clear plastic needs a darker backdrop to stay visible.
Strong text/image separation: black headline, green highlight phrases at the start of lines, body 24px, and the green call-out box is solid, so it is readable over any photo.
weak_spots: Photographs are AI-generated. They were checked for warped hands, objects and gibberish text, but a final human look at full size is sensible, especially slide 2 (hands, bottle, machine lettering) and slide 3 (gloves).

Slide 2 shows a generic, unbranded reverse vending machine (RVM) with 'DRS' and 'Deposit Refund Scheme' lettering. It is one common type of return point and not any specific scheme's hardware; a DRS can also use manual return points.

The images illustrate stages. They do not show that any particular packaging is recycled into a bottle. The new bottle on slide 4 is generic and could be read as bottle-to-bottle recycling, which the copy does not claim; if that is a concern, swap it for another recycled-material product.

slides.title: Slide 1 – Value is at risk after consumption
slides.says: Packaging can retain value, but littering, improper disposal and gaps in collection stop it reaching recovery channels. Recovering that value needs a more organised collection system and a clear pathway to material recovery.
shows: A low kerbside view of an ordinary Indian street: a modest scatter of empty bottles and cans beside a storm-drain grating.
Parked scooters and passers-by recede into soft focus: everyday leakage, not a dump.
The photograph is panned so the litter sits between the body copy and the green call-out box.
icons: No heaps or landfill drama: realistic and credible.
The solution statement, solid green for contrast.

slides.title: Slide 2 – A Deposit Refund Scheme creates a structured return pathway
slides.says: A DRS uses a nominal refundable deposit to encourage the return of eligible empty packaging, channelling it into organised collection systems where it can move towards recycling.
shows: A customer feeds an empty PET bottle into the round aperture of a modern reverse vending machine at a supermarket entrance.
The machine carries only 'DRS' and 'Deposit Refund Scheme', with bottle and can pictograms and no other branding.
The machine and customer take the right half; the copy sits on white on the left.
icons: A familiar DRS return point, shown generically.
Bottle and can: what is eligible, without claiming specifics.
The act of returning, which is the centre of the scheme.

slides.title: Slide 3 – Material quality matters for recovery
slides.says: How packaging is collected and handled affects its suitability for recycling. Contamination and poor handling can reduce material quality and limit the value that can be recovered.
shows: Gloved hands sort bottles at a table between two crates at a collection centre.
Left crate: clean, empty, dry bottles. Right crate: bottles with residue and food-soiled wrappers.
Same table, same hands: the only difference is how the material was collected and handled.
icons: The contrast the slide is about, readable at a glance.
Handling is a human step, not an abstract one.
Kept short on this slide so the clean crate is not washed out.

slides.title: Slide 4 – Building a better pathway keeps material value in circulation
slides.says: DRS helps strengthen the return and collection of eligible packaging. Effective sorting, processing and recycling help turn collected material into a usable resource. The goal is for packaging waste to find its way back into the value chain.
shows: Three stages on one bench, read left to right: a used, empty bottle that has been crushed by hand but is clean, as a consumer would return it; a clean mound of processed flakes; and a new, clear bottle standing behind them.
The used bottle is deliberately not dirty: packaging coming back through a DRS comes straight from the consumer.
A dark, softly blurred plant backdrop sits behind the objects so the clear plastic keeps its edges and highlights; it fades to white on the copy side.
icons: Crushed, clean, with the same teal cap as the litter on slide 1, so the story comes full circle.
The processing step in the middle, so the 'new' bottle is not shown as the same bottle returning.
Material value back in use. Kept plain and generic.
The goal in the green call-out.
